notes.front: What is an Azure managed disk?
notes.back: A block-level storage volume for Azure virtual machines that Azure manages; you choose only its type and size.
notes.explanation: After you provision the disk, Azure handles the rest.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disks overview” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure managed disks are block-level storage volumes managed by Azure and used with Azure Virtual Machines. Managed disks are like physical disks in an on-premises server, but they're virtualized. With managed disks, you only have to specify the disk type and the disk size, then provision the disk.
notes.example: Like ordering a server disk by size and speed, without ever handling the storage behind it.

notes.front: What is a managed disk snapshot?
notes.back: A read-only, crash-consistent full copy of one managed disk, taken at a point in time.
notes.explanation: It is stored as a standard managed disk by default and lets you back up a disk at any moment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disks overview”, “Managed disk snapshots” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A managed disk snapshot is a read-only, crash-consistent full copy of a managed disk that's stored as a standard managed disk by default. With snapshots, you can back up your managed disks at any point in time.
notes.example: Like photocopying a ledger before a risky edit, so you can go back to the copy.

notes.front: What is a local temporary disk on an Azure virtual machine?
notes.back: Storage provisioned locally on the machine’s host rather than in remote Azure Storage, for data you needn’t keep.
notes.explanation: It is best suited to caches, buffers and temporary files.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Virtual machines in Azure”, “Local temporary storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Local temporary storage uses additional disks provisioned directly as local storage to an Azure virtual machine host, rather than on remote Azure Storage. This type of storage is best suited for data that does not need to be retained permanently, such as caches, buffers, and temporary files.
notes.example: Like a whiteboard in a meeting room: handy while you work, wiped when you leave.

notes.front: What is encryption at host?
notes.back: A virtual machine option that encrypts data stored on the host at rest and sends it encrypted to Azure Storage.
notes.explanation: It gives end-to-end encryption for the machine’s disk data.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal to enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable encryption at host, data stored on the VM host is encrypted at rest and flows encrypted to the Storage service.
notes.example: Like sealing a letter before it leaves the office, not only once it reaches the archive.

notes.front: What is a disk encryption set (DES)?
notes.back: The resource that lets managed disk encryption use customer-managed keys.
notes.explanation: Server-side encryption of managed disks supports customer-managed keys when configured with one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of managed disk encryption options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you configure it with a disk encryption set (DES), it also supports customer-managed keys.
notes.example: Like a key ring that tells the disk service which of your own keys to lock the disks with.

notes.front: What is Azure Resource Mover?
notes.back: A service that moves Azure resources between Azure regions.
notes.explanation: It gives a single hub for moving resources across regions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Resource Mover?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Resource Mover helps you to move Azure resources between Azure regions.
notes.example: Like a removals firm for relocating a workload from one region to another.

notes.front: In an availability set, what is a fault domain?
notes.back: A group of virtual machines that share a common power source and network switch.
notes.explanation: By default, the machines in an availability set are separated across up to three fault domains.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “Fault domains” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Fault domains define the group of virtual machines that share a common power source and network switch. By default, the virtual machines configured within your availability set are separated across up to three fault domains.
notes.example: Like the servers in one rack, fed by the same power strip and switch.

notes.front: In an availability set, what is an update domain?
notes.back: A group of virtual machines and underlying hardware that can be restarted at the same time.
notes.explanation: Planned maintenance restarts machines one update domain at a time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “Update domains” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Update domains indicate groups of virtual machines and underlying physical hardware that can be restarted at the same time.
notes.example: Like one wing of a hospital closed for repainting while the other wings stay open.

notes.front: What is autoscale for a Virtual Machine Scale Set?
notes.back: Rules that increase or decrease the number of virtual machines in the scale set as demand changes.
notes.explanation: You configure the rules when increased or decreased load is consistent rather than brief.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Benefits of autoscale” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If this increased load is consistent, rather than just a brief demand, you can configure autoscale rules to increase and decrease the number of virtual machines in the scale set.
notes.example: Like a supermarket opening extra tills while queues stay long and closing them once they clear.

notes.front: What is scheduled autoscale?
notes.back: Autoscale rules that change the number of virtual machines at fixed times.
notes.explanation: The rules are based on a schedule rather than on performance metrics.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Scheduled autoscale” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can also create autoscale rules based on schedules. These schedule-based rules allow you to automatically scale the number of virtual machines at fixed times.
notes.example: Like rostering extra staff every Monday morning, whether or not the queue has formed yet.

notes.front: In the Azure portal, on the Virtual machines page, what do you select to start creating a virtual machine?
notes.back: Create, then Virtual machine from the drop-down.
notes.explanation: That opens the Create a virtual machine page.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Create a Windows virtual machine in the Azure portal”, “Create virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the **Virtual machines** page, select **Create** from the menu at the top of the page and then select **Virtual machine** from the drop-down. The **Create a virtual machine** page opens.

notes.front: On Create a virtual machine, you enter a name and choose an image. What does the page do with the other fields?
notes.back: Fills them with defaults and names the other needed resources after the virtual machine.
notes.explanation: You can accept those defaults and change only what you need.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Create a Windows virtual machine in the Azure portal”, “Create virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The page will fill in the other fields with defaults and use the VM name to create similar names for the other resources that are needed.

notes.front: When creating a Windows virtual machine in the portal, how long must the administrator password be?
notes.back: At least 12 characters, and it must meet the complexity requirements.
notes.explanation: The password goes with the username under Administrator account.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Create a Windows virtual machine in the Azure portal”, “Create virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The password must be at least 12 characters long and meet the defined complexity requirements.

notes.front: You are creating a test virtual machine in the portal and want it to switch itself off every evening. Where do you set this?
notes.back: On the Management tab, under Auto-shutdown: Enable auto-shutdown.
notes.choices:
A) Basics tab, Instance details
B) Disks tab
C) Management tab, Auto-shutdown
D) After creation only, with a script
notes.choicesExplained: A holds the name and image. B holds disk settings. D is wrong: the option is on the creation page.
notes.explanation: You then pick a shutdown time and time zone.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Create a Windows virtual machine in the Azure portal”, “Create virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: select the **Management** tab. 1. In the **Auto-shutdown** section, select the **Enable auto-shutdown** option.

notes.front: What are two aspects of a virtual machine to decide before you create it?
notes.back: Among others: its size and its location.
notes.explanation: The documentation also lists names, the operating system, configuration after start-up, related resources and the maximum number of machines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Virtual machines in Azure”, “What do I need to think about before creating a virtual machine?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: These aspects of a virtual machine are important to think about before you start: * The names of your resources * The location where the resources are stored * The size of the virtual machine

notes.front: By default, which resource group are a new virtual machine’s supporting resources created in?
notes.back: The same resource group as the virtual machine.
notes.explanation: Those resources, such as the virtual network, come with their own costs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Virtual machines in Azure”, “Parts of a VM and how they’re billed” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, these resources are created in the same resource group as the VM.

notes.front: Which managed disk encryption is always enabled, encrypting data as it persists on the storage clusters?
notes.back: Azure Disk Storage server-side encryption.
notes.explanation: It is also called encryption at rest or Azure Storage encryption.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of managed disk encryption options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Azure Disk Storage server-side encryption** (also referred to as encryption at rest or Azure Storage encryption) is always enabled. It automatically encrypts data stored on Azure managed disks (OS and data disks) when it persists data on the storage clusters.

notes.front: Server-side encryption or encryption at host: which also encrypts temp disks and disk caches?
notes.back: Encryption at host. Server-side encryption doesn’t cover temp disks or caches.
notes.explanation: Encryption at host enhances server-side encryption so temp disks and caches are encrypted at rest and flow encrypted to storage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of managed disk encryption options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Encryption at host** is a virtual machine option that enhances Azure Disk Storage server-side encryption. This option ensures that all temp disks and disk caches are encrypted at rest and flow encrypted to the storage clusters.

notes.front: Which managed disk encryption option encrypts the disks inside the virtual machine, using BitLocker on Windows or `DM-Crypt` on Linux?
notes.back: Azure Disk Encryption.
notes.explanation: It works with Azure Key Vault to control the disk encryption keys and secrets.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of managed disk encryption options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: ADE encrypts the OS and data disks of Azure virtual machines (VMs) inside your VMs by using the DM-Crypt feature of Linux or the BitLocker feature of Windows. ADE is integrated with Azure Key Vault

notes.front: When is Azure Disk Encryption scheduled to retire, and what should new virtual machines use instead?
notes.back: 15 September 2028; use encryption at host for new machines.
notes.explanation: Confidential virtual machine sizes are the suggested alternative for confidential computing workloads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of managed disk encryption options”, “Comparison” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Disk Encryption is scheduled for retirement on **September 15, 2028**. Use encryption at host for new VMs, or consider Confidential VM sizes with OS disk encryption for confidential computing workloads.

notes.front: Which disk encryption option binds its keys to the virtual machine’s trusted platform module, so only that machine can read the protected disk?
notes.back: Confidential disk encryption.
notes.explanation: It protects the operating system disk, and encryption at host can cover the other disks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of managed disk encryption options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: binds disk encryption keys to the virtual machine's TPM and makes the protected disk content accessible only to the VM.

notes.front: With encryption at host, temporary disks and ephemeral operating system disks are encrypted at rest with {{c1::platform-managed keys}}.
notes.explanation: Disk caches, by contrast, use whichever kind of key their disk uses.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal to enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Temporary disks and ephemeral OS disks are encrypted at rest with platform-managed keys when you enable end-to-end encryption.

notes.front: With encryption at host, which kind of key encrypts a disk’s cache?
notes.back: The same kind as the disk: customer-managed for a disk with customer-managed keys, otherwise platform-managed.
notes.explanation: The cache follows the disk encryption type you selected.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal to enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The OS and data disk caches are encrypted at rest with either customer-managed or platform-managed keys, depending on the selected disk encryption type.

notes.front: A new virtual machine must have its temp disk and disk caches encrypted, and data encrypted between compute and storage. Which option do you enable?
notes.back: Encryption at host.
notes.choices:
A) Server-side encryption only
B) Encryption at host
C) Azure Disk Encryption
D) A managed disk snapshot
notes.choicesExplained: A doesn’t encrypt temp disks or caches. C is scheduled for retirement, and encryption at host is advised for new machines. D is a backup copy, not encryption.
notes.explanation: Server-side encryption alone doesn’t encrypt temp disks or caches, and Azure Disk Encryption is retiring, with encryption at host advised for new machines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of managed disk encryption options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This option ensures that all temp disks and disk caches are encrypted at rest and flow encrypted to the storage clusters.

notes.front: What must be done for a subscription before any virtual machine in it can use encryption at host?
notes.back: The EncryptionAtHost feature must be registered for the subscription.
notes.explanation: Registration can take a few minutes; confirm it shows Registered first.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal to enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You must enable the feature for your subscription before you can use encryption at host for either your VM or Virtual Machine Scale Set.

notes.front: What must you do to a virtual machine before you can disable encryption at host?
notes.back: Deallocate it.
notes.explanation: Encryption at host can’t be disabled while the machine is allocated.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal to enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host”, “Disable encryption at host” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Deallocate your VM first, encryption at host can't be disabled unless your VM is deallocated.

notes.front: When creating a virtual machine in the portal, on which pane do you select Encryption at host?
notes.back: The Disks pane.
notes.explanation: You choose a region and a supported size on Basics first.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal to enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host”, “Deploy a VM with platform-managed keys” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Fill in the other values on the **Basic** pane as you like, and then proceed to the **Disks** pane. 1. On the **Disks** pane, select **Encryption at host**.

notes.front: You want a new virtual machine to use encryption at host with your own keys. The feature is registered. What must you set up before deploying?
notes.back: An Azure Key Vault and a disk encryption set.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more: select Encryption at host
B) An Azure Key Vault and a disk encryption set
C) Azure Disk Encryption on the machine
D) A storage account for the keys
notes.choicesExplained: A gives platform-managed keys, not yours. C is a different, retiring option. D is not what the procedure asks for.
notes.explanation: Then, on the Disks pane, you select Encryption at host and pick your customer-managed key under Key management.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal to enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host”, “Create an Azure Key Vault and disk encryption set” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Once the feature is enabled, you need to set up an Azure Key Vault and a disk encryption set, if you haven't already.

notes.front: In the ordinary case, which Azure CLI command moves a virtual machine to another resource group or subscription?
notes.back: az resource move.
notes.explanation: In Azure PowerShell the equivalent is Move-AzResource.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For Azure CLI, use the az resource move command. For Azure PowerShell, use the Move-AzResource command.

notes.front: What are the three virtual machine features that need a workaround before the machine can move to another resource group or subscription?
notes.back: Disk encryption, a Marketplace plan, and Azure Backup.
notes.explanation: Every other scenario uses the standard move operations.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your virtual machine uses disk encryption, a Marketplace plan, or Azure Backup, you must use one of the workarounds described in this article.

notes.front: Can a virtual machine in an availability set be moved on its own?
notes.back: No. Machines in an availability set can’t be moved individually.
notes.explanation: It is one of the listed scenarios not yet supported.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription”, “Scenarios not supported” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Virtual machines in an availability set can't be moved individually.

notes.front: When can a virtual machine in an existing virtual network move to a new subscription?
notes.back: Only when the virtual network and all its dependent resources move too.
notes.explanation: The machine can’t leave its network behind in the old subscription.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription”, “Scenarios not supported” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Virtual machines in an existing virtual network can be moved to a new subscription only when the virtual network and all of its dependent resources are also moved.

notes.front: Can a virtual machine created from a Marketplace resource with a plan be moved to another subscription?
notes.back: No. The workaround is to deprovision it and deploy it again in the new subscription.
notes.explanation: The workaround might not work in every scenario, for example if the plan is no longer offered.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription”, “Virtual machines with Marketplace plans” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Virtual machines created from Marketplace resources with plans attached can't be moved across subscriptions. To work around this limitation, you can deprovision the virtual machine in the current subscription, and deploy it again in the new subscription.

notes.front: A virtual machine uses Azure Disk Encryption. How does moving it to another resource group differ from moving it to another subscription?
notes.back: Another resource group: allowed once deallocated. Another subscription: you must disable encryption first.
notes.explanation: The subscription move is the one that needs encryption turned off.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription”, “Azure disk encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: can be moved to another resource group when it is in deallocated state. However, to move such virtual machine to another subscription, you must disable encryption.

notes.front: A running virtual machine protected by Azure Disk Encryption must move to a different subscription. What must you do first?
notes.back: Disable its encryption.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: move it as it is
B) Only deallocate it
C) Disable its encryption
D) Move it with Azure Resource Mover
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the encryption rule. B is enough only for a move to another resource group. D moves resources between regions.
notes.explanation: A machine with Azure Disk Encryption can only move to another subscription once encryption is disabled.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription”, “Azure disk encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: However, to move such virtual machine to another subscription, you must disable encryption.

notes.front: Before moving a virtual machine configured with Azure Backup, what must you delete?
notes.back: Its restore point collections (snapshots) in the vault.
notes.explanation: Restore points already copied to the vault can be kept and moved.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Handling special cases when moving virtual machines to resource group or subscription”, “Virtual machines with Azure Backup” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To move virtual machines configured with Azure Backup, you must delete the restore points collections (snapshots) from the vault. Restore points already copied to the vault can be retained and moved.

notes.front: Which role do you need on the subscription to add resources to a region move in Azure Resource Mover?
notes.back: Owner.
notes.explanation: Resource Mover creates a managed identity and assigns it Contributor or User Access Administrator in the source subscription, and making that assignment needs Owner permissions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure VMs across regions”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To create the identity, and to assign it the required role (Contributor or User Access administrator in the source subscription), the account you use to add resources needs *Owner* permissions on the subscription.

notes.front: When Azure Resource Mover finds that a resource depends on others, what are your two options?
notes.back: Move the dependent resources too, or use equivalent resources in the target region.
notes.explanation: Resource Mover validates the selected resources and resolves their dependencies before the move.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Resource Mover?”, “Move across regions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If there are dependencies, you have a couple of options: - Move the dependent resources to the target region. - Don't move the dependent resources but use equivalent resources in the target region instead.

notes.front: In Azure Resource Mover, what happens to a source virtual machine when you initiate the move?
notes.back: It is shut down while replica machines are created in the target region; some downtime occurs, usually minutes.
notes.explanation: Afterwards the resources are in the Commit move pending state.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure VMs across regions”, “Initiate the move” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For VMs, replica VMs are created in the target region. The source VM is shut down, and some downtime occurs (usually minutes).

notes.front: After the initial move in Azure Resource Mover, what is the difference between Commit and Discard?
notes.back: Commit completes the move (source goes to Delete source pending); Discard returns the resource to Initiate move pending.
notes.explanation: You might discard when testing and you don’t want to move the source for real.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure VMs across regions”, “Commit or discard the move” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Discard**: You might discard a move if you're testing, and you don't want to actually move the source resource. Discarding the move returns the resource to a state of *Initiate move pending*. - **Commit**: Commit completes the move to the target region.

notes.front: After you commit a region move in Azure Resource Mover, is the source resource deleted?
notes.back: Not automatically. It enters Delete source pending, and you decide whether to delete it.
notes.explanation: Committing doesn’t affect the source virtual machine or its networking resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure VMs across regions”, “Commit or discard the move” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After committing, a source resource will be in a state of *Delete source pending*, and you can decide if you want to delete it.

notes.front: You ran an initial region move in Azure Resource Mover only to test the process, and you don’t want the machine to move. What do you do?
notes.back: Discard the move.
notes.choices:
A) Commit the move
B) Discard the move
C) Delete the source resource
D) Deallocate the target machine
notes.choicesExplained: A completes the move. C removes the original, the opposite of what you want. D leaves the move in progress.
notes.explanation: Discarding returns the resource to Initiate move pending instead of completing the move.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure VMs across regions”, “Commit or discard the move” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Discard**: You might discard a move if you're testing, and you don't want to actually move the source resource.

notes.front: When you move a single-instance virtual machine from regional to zonal deployment, what happens to the source machine?
notes.back: It is stopped, with brief downtime, while a zonal copy is created and started; it stays stopped afterwards.
notes.explanation: You can then delete the source machine or keep it for another purpose.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure single-instance virtual machines from regional to zonal availability”, “Portal: Review VM properties before move” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The source VM is **stopped**, so brief downtime occurs. - A target zonal VM is created and started.

notes.front: Changing the size of a running virtual machine will cause it to {{c1::restart}}.
notes.explanation: So resizing should be treated as a disruptive operation, especially for stateful workloads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Even when deallocation isn’t required, changing the size of a running VM will cause it to restart. For this reason, resizing a VM should be considered a disruptive operation, especially for stateful workloads.

notes.front: When may you have to deallocate a virtual machine before resizing it?
notes.back: When the new size isn’t available on the hardware cluster currently hosting it.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the resize works whether the machine is running or deallocated.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In some cases, you must deallocate the VM before resizing. Deallocation may be required if the new size isn’t available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the VM.

notes.front: What does deallocating a virtual machine release, and what does it leave alone?
notes.back: It releases any dynamic IP addresses; the operating system and data disks aren’t affected.
notes.explanation: The disks keep their data; only the dynamic addresses are released.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Deallocating the VM also releases any dynamic IP addresses assigned to the VM. The OS and data disks are not affected.

notes.front: A virtual machine in an availability set needs a size that isn’t on its current hardware cluster. What must you deallocate?
notes.back: All the virtual machines in the availability set.
notes.explanation: You might also need to resize the other machines in the set afterwards.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine”, “Change the VM size” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the new size for a VM in an availability set isn't available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the VM, then you need to deallocate all VMs in the availability set to resize the VM.

notes.front: In the Azure portal, where do you change a virtual machine’s size?
notes.back: Under Availability + scale, select Size, pick a new size and select Resize.
notes.explanation: If the size you want isn’t listed while the machine runs, stopping it may reveal more sizes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine”, “Change the VM size” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the left menu, in the **Availability + scale** section, select **size**. 1. Pick a new compatible size from the list of available sizes and then select **Resize**.

notes.front: Your virtual machine is running and the size you want isn’t in the portal’s list. What might reveal more sizes?
notes.back: Stopping the virtual machine.
notes.explanation: The documentation suggests stopping the machine when the size you want isn’t listed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine”, “Change the VM size” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your VM is still running and you don't see the size you want in the list, stopping the virtual machine may reveal more sizes.

notes.front: A resize fails. What size does the portal then show, and what size is the machine actually running?
notes.back: The portal shows the requested size; the machine keeps running on its previous size.
notes.explanation: The displayed size reflects the latest applied configuration, not the actual running size.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If a resize operation fails, the VM model will still display the requested size, but the VM will continue running on its previous size until the resize is successfully allocated.

notes.front: Can a Windows virtual machine be resized from a size with a local temporary disk to a size without one?
notes.back: No. On Windows, both sizes must have a local temp disk, or both must lack one.
notes.explanation: Linux machines can resize between the two kinds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine”, “Limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Resizing between VM sizes that have a local temp disk and VM sizes that have no local temp disk is supported for Linux VMs. For Windows VMs, only the following resize combinations are allowed:

notes.front: When resizing a virtual machine that uses Premium Storage, which version of a size should you pick?
notes.back: An “s” version, such as Standard_E4s_v3 rather than Standard_E4_v3.
notes.explanation: The s version is the one with Premium Storage support.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine”, “Choose the right SKU” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your VM uses Premium Storage, make sure that you choose an **s** version of the size to get Premium Storage support.

notes.front: A production virtual machine is running, and the larger size you need is available on its current cluster. Will resizing it interrupt users?
notes.back: Yes. Resizing a running machine restarts it, even without deallocation.
notes.choices:
A) No: the size is on the same cluster
B) Yes: the machine restarts
C) Only if it has data disks
D) Only if it is in an availability set
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses deallocation with restart: no deallocation is needed, but the machine still restarts. C and D have no bearing on the restart.
notes.explanation: Resizing should be considered a disruptive operation, especially for stateful workloads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Even when deallocation isn’t required, changing the size of a running VM will cause it to restart.

notes.front: You deallocate a virtual machine to resize it. Afterwards, clients using its old dynamic public address can’t reach it, though its disks are intact. Why?
notes.back: Deallocating released its dynamic IP address.
notes.choices:
A) The resize deleted its network interface
B) Deallocation released its dynamic address
C) Its disks were reset
D) The new size doesn’t support public addresses
notes.choicesExplained: A is not something a resize does. C contradicts the scenario and the documentation. D is not a documented cause.
notes.explanation: Deallocation releases dynamic addresses but doesn’t affect the operating system or data disks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Change the size of a virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Deallocating the VM also releases any dynamic IP addresses assigned to the VM. The OS and data disks are not affected.

notes.front: Which type of virtual machine size offers a balanced processor-to-memory ratio, for development and testing and small to medium databases?
notes.back: General purpose.
notes.explanation: It also suits low to medium traffic web servers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Sizes for virtual machines in Azure”, “General purpose” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: General purpose VM sizes provide balanced CPU-to-memory ratio. Ideal for testing and development, small to medium databases, and low to medium traffic web servers.

notes.front: Which type of virtual machine size has a high processor-to-memory ratio, suiting batch processes and network appliances?
notes.back: Compute optimized.
notes.explanation: It also suits medium traffic web servers and application servers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Sizes for virtual machines in Azure”, “Compute optimized” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Compute optimized VM sizes have a high CPU-to-memory ratio. These sizes are good for medium traffic web servers, network appliances, batch processes, and application servers.

notes.front: Which type of virtual machine size has a high memory-to-processor ratio, suiting relational database servers and in-memory analytics?
notes.back: Memory optimized.
notes.explanation: It also suits medium to large caches.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Sizes for virtual machines in Azure”, “Memory optimized” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Memory optimized VM sizes offer a high memory-to-CPU ratio that is great for relational database servers, medium to large caches, and in-memory analytics.

notes.front: Which type of virtual machine size offers high disk throughput, suiting big data and data warehousing?
notes.back: Storage optimized.
notes.explanation: It also suits large transactional databases.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Sizes for virtual machines in Azure”, “Storage optimized” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Storage optimized virtual machine (VM) sizes offer high disk throughput and IO, and are ideal for Big Data, SQL, NoSQL databases, data warehousing, and large transactional databases.

notes.front: A virtual machine runs a relational database and keeps running short of memory, while its processors sit mostly idle. Which type of size should you resize to?
notes.back: Memory optimized.
notes.choices:
A) Compute optimized
B) Memory optimized
C) Storage optimized
D) General purpose
notes.choicesExplained: A adds processors, not memory. C adds disk throughput. D keeps the balanced ratio that is already short of memory.
notes.explanation: Memory optimized sizes have a high memory-to-processor ratio and suit relational database servers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Sizes for virtual machines in Azure”, “Memory optimized” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Memory optimized VM sizes offer a high memory-to-CPU ratio that is great for relational database servers, medium to large caches, and in-memory analytics.

notes.front: In an Azure virtual machine size name, what does the feature letter “p” indicate?
notes.back: An Arm-based processor, such as Microsoft Cobalt or Ampere Altra.
notes.explanation: With no processor letter, the series uses Intel x86-64 processors.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Sizes for virtual machines in Azure”, “Name structure breakdown” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If no feature letter for a CPU is listed, the series uses Intel x86-64 CPUs. If the CPU is AMD, it's listed as `a`. If the CPU is ARM based (Microsoft Cobalt or Ampere Altra), it's listed as `p`.

notes.front: How many replicas of your data do managed disks keep?
notes.back: Three.
notes.explanation: If one or two replicas have problems, the remaining ones help keep your data.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disks overview”, “Azure managed disk durability and availability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To achieve this availability, managed disks provide three replicas of your data. If one or two replicas experience problems, the remaining replicas help ensure persistence of your data and high tolerance against failures.

notes.front: Which managed disk type is the highest-performing option, suited to data-intensive workloads such as top-tier databases?
notes.back: Ultra Disk.
notes.explanation: Its performance parameters can be changed without restarting the virtual machine.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Ultra Disks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Ultra Disks are the highest-performing storage option for Azure virtual machines (VMs). You can change the performance parameters of an Ultra Disk without having to restart your VMs.

notes.front: Can an Ultra Disk be used as a virtual machine’s operating system disk?
notes.back: No. Ultra Disks must be data disks and can only be created empty.
notes.explanation: Premium solid-state drives are suggested for the operating system disk alongside them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Ultra Disks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Ultra Disks must be used as data disks and can only be created as empty disks. When using Ultra Disks as data disks, use Premium solid-state drives (SSDs) as operating system (OS) disks.

notes.front: Which managed disk type has no fixed sizes and lets you adjust performance without downtime, but doesn’t support host caching?
notes.back: Premium SSD v2.
notes.explanation: You can set its capacity, throughput and performance individually at any time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Differences between Premium SSD and Premium SSD v2” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Unlike Premium SSDs, Premium SSD v2 doesn't have dedicated sizes. You can set a Premium SSD v2 to any supported size you prefer, and make granular adjustments to the performance without downtime. Premium SSD v2 doesn't support host caching

notes.front: Which managed disk type suits mission-critical production applications but works only with compatible virtual machine series?
notes.back: Premium SSD.
notes.explanation: Its capacity and performance are guaranteed once provisioned.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Premium SSDs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Premium SSDs are suitable for mission-critical production applications, but you can use them only with compatible VM series.

notes.front: Which managed disk type suits web servers, lightly used enterprise applications, and development and test environments?
notes.back: Standard SSD.
notes.explanation: It is optimised for workloads that need consistent performance at lower performance levels.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Compare Azure managed disk types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Web servers, lightly used enterprise applications, and development and test environments.

notes.front: Which managed disk type suits backup and other noncritical, infrequently accessed workloads?
notes.back: Standard HDD.
notes.explanation: It isn’t suitable for workloads that need low latency, such as transactional databases.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Compare Azure managed disk types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Backup and other noncritical, infrequently accessed workloads.

notes.front: A transaction-heavy database needs the highest disk performance, on a data disk. Which disk type fits?
notes.back: Ultra Disk.
notes.choices:
A) Ultra Disk
B) Standard SSD
C) Standard HDD
D) The local temporary disk
notes.choicesExplained: B is for web servers and light enterprise use. C is for backup and infrequent access. D isn’t kept and isn’t a managed disk type.
notes.explanation: Ultra Disks are aimed at I/O-intensive workloads such as top-tier databases and transaction-heavy workloads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Ultra Disks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Ultra Disks are suited for data-intensive workloads such as SAP HANA, top-tier databases, and transaction-heavy workloads.

notes.front: You need a cheap disk for backup files that are rarely read and aren’t latency-sensitive. Which disk type fits?
notes.back: Standard HDD.
notes.choices:
A) Ultra Disk
B) Premium SSD v2
C) Premium SSD
D) Standard HDD
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are aimed at production or performance-sensitive workloads.
notes.explanation: Standard HDD is the type for backup and other noncritical, infrequently accessed workloads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disk types”, “Compare Azure managed disk types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Backup and other noncritical, infrequently accessed workloads.

notes.front: What happens to data on a local temporary disk when its virtual machine is deallocated or deleted?
notes.back: It is lost.
notes.explanation: Data on these disks isn’t backed up; the storage is recreated on startup.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Virtual machines in Azure”, “Local temporary storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Since data stored on these disks isn't backed up, it's lost when the VM is deallocated or deleted. The ephemeral storage is recreated on startup.

notes.front: Does data on a virtual machine’s temporary disk survive a successful standard restart?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: It can be lost during a maintenance event, a redeploy, or when the machine is stopped.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disks overview”, “Temporary disk” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data on the temporary disk might be lost during a maintenance event, when you redeploy a VM, or when you stop the VM. During a successful standard restart of the VM, data on the temporary disk persists.

notes.front: On a Windows virtual machine, which drive is the temporary disk by default?
notes.back: Drive D.
notes.explanation: The temporary disk isn’t a managed disk.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disks overview”, “Temporary disk” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On Windows VMs, the temporary disk is drive D by default.

notes.front: An application on a Windows virtual machine saves customers’ uploaded documents to drive D. What is the risk?
notes.back: Drive D is the temporary disk, so the documents can be lost, for example when the machine is deallocated.
notes.choices:
A) None: drive D is a managed data disk
B) The documents can be lost
C) Drive D fills the operating system disk
D) The documents are only readable by administrators
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: on Windows, drive D is the temporary disk by default. C and D aren’t documented effects.
notes.explanation: Temporary storage suits caches and temporary files; application data belongs on a data disk.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Virtual machines in Azure”, “Local temporary storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This type of storage is best suited for data that does not need to be retained permanently, such as caches, buffers, and temporary files. Since data stored on these disks isn't backed up, it's lost when the VM is deallocated or deleted.

notes.front: Where should applications and their data generally be stored on an Azure virtual machine?
notes.back: On data disks, not on the operating system disk.
notes.explanation: The operating system disk is best kept for operating system information.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disks overview”, “OS disk” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Generally, you should store only your OS information on the OS disk. The data disk is where you should store all applications and data.

notes.front: In the portal, on a virtual machine’s Disks pane, which option adds a brand-new data disk?
notes.back: Create and attach a new disk.
notes.explanation: You then choose the disk’s settings and name, and select Save.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Attach a managed data disk to a Windows VM by using the Azure portal”, “Add a data disk” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On the **Disks** pane, select **Create and attach a new disk**.

notes.front: A Windows virtual machine needs extra storage for a new application’s data. You add a disk in the portal. What must you still do inside the machine?
notes.back: Initialise and format the new disk, for example in Disk Management.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the disk is ready as drive D
B) Initialise and format it
C) Restart the machine twice
D) Expand the operating system disk
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: drive D is the temporary disk, and the new disk arrives uninitialised. C and D don’t prepare the new disk.
notes.explanation: A newly attached empty disk appears uninitialised until you initialise and format it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Attach a managed data disk to a Windows VM by using the Azure portal”, “Initialize a new data disk” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Disk Management recognizes that you have a new, uninitialized disk and the **Initialize Disk** window appears.

notes.front: Should you initialise and format a data disk that already holds data?
notes.back: No. Only a newly created, empty disk; otherwise the data may become inaccessible or be erased.
notes.explanation: Check the disk number and size first to be sure you have the right disk.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Attach a managed data disk to a Windows VM by using the Azure portal”, “Initialize a new data disk” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Initialize and format only a newly created, empty data disk. If the disk was previously used or contains existing data, initializing, repartitioning, or formatting it might make the data inaccessible or permanently erase it.

notes.front: Shrinking an existing managed disk {{c1::isn’t supported}} and might result in data loss.
notes.explanation: Disks can be made larger, never smaller.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Shrinking an existing disk isn't supported and might result in data loss.

notes.front: Unless it qualifies for expanding without downtime, what does enlarging a data disk require?
notes.back: The virtual machine must be deallocated.
notes.explanation: Only eligible data disks can be expanded while the machine keeps running.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Unless you use Expand without downtime, expanding a data disk requires the VM to be deallocated.

notes.front: Can an operating system disk be expanded without deallocating the virtual machine?
notes.back: No. Only eligible data disks can; operating system disks need deallocation.
notes.explanation: Data disks that don’t meet the requirements need deallocation too.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows virtual machine”, “Resize a managed disk in the Azure portal” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Only eligible data disks can be expanded without deallocating the VM. OS disks and data disks that don't meet the requirements for expansion without downtime require deallocation.

notes.front: In the portal, where do you enlarge a managed disk once you have opened it from the virtual machine’s Disks page?
notes.back: Size + performance: pick a larger size and select Resize.
notes.explanation: The new size should be greater than the existing one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows virtual machine”, “Resize a managed disk in the Azure portal” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On **Size + performance**, select the disk size that you want. The new size should be greater than the existing disk size.

notes.front: After you enlarge a managed disk in Azure, what else must you do to use the extra space?
notes.back: Expand the volume inside the operating system.
notes.explanation: Enlarging the disk alone doesn’t let the operating system use the new space.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you expand the disks, expand the volume in the OS to take advantage of the larger disk.

notes.front: To save money, a colleague wants to cut a 1 TiB managed data disk down to 512 GiB in the portal. What happens?
notes.back: It can’t be done: shrinking a managed disk isn’t supported.
notes.choices:
A) It works after deallocating the machine
B) It works while the machine runs
C) It isn’t supported
D) It works after taking a snapshot
notes.choicesExplained: A and B describe expansion rules, not shrinking. D is not a documented exception.
notes.explanation: Shrinking isn’t supported and might result in data loss; only expansion is.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows virtual machine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Shrinking an existing disk isn't supported and might result in data loss.

notes.front: A running virtual machine’s operating system disk is nearly full and you plan to enlarge it in the portal. What must you do first?
notes.back: Stop (deallocate) the virtual machine.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: expand it while it runs
B) Stop (deallocate) the machine
C) Take the disk offline in Windows only
D) Attach a second operating system disk
notes.choicesExplained: A applies only to eligible data disks. C doesn’t deallocate the machine. D isn’t possible: a machine has one operating system disk.
notes.explanation: Operating system disks can’t be expanded without deallocation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Expand virtual hard disks attached to a Windows virtual machine”, “Resize a managed disk in the Azure portal” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: OS disks and data disks that don't meet the requirements for expansion without downtime require deallocation.

notes.front: Does a managed disk snapshot depend on its source disk?
notes.back: No. Snapshots exist independently of the source disk and can be used to create new managed disks.
notes.explanation: You can back up a managed disk at any point in time with one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure managed disks overview”, “Managed disk snapshots” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: These snapshots exist independently of the source disk, and you can use them to create new managed disks.

notes.front: At most, how many fault domains and update domains can an availability set have?
notes.back: Up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains.
notes.explanation: The platform assigns each machine in the set one of each.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “How do availability sets work?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The underlying Azure platform assigns an *update domain* and a *fault domain* to each virtual machine in your availability set. Each availability set can have up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains.

notes.front: Can you change an availability set’s fault domain and update domain counts after creating it?
notes.back: No. They are fixed once the set is created.
notes.explanation: So choose the counts when you create the set.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “How do availability sets work?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each availability set can have up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains. These settings can't be changed after the availability set is created.

notes.front: An availability set was created with two fault domains. A year later you want three for the same set. What can you do?
notes.back: Nothing in place: the fault and update domain counts can’t be changed after the set is created.
notes.choices:
A) Edit the count in the Azure portal
B) Change it with the Azure CLI
C) Deallocate the machines, then change it
D) It can’t be changed on the existing set
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C all assume the count can be edited, but it is fixed once the set exists.
notes.explanation: The counts are fixed at creation, whatever tool you use.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “How do availability sets work?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each availability set can have up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains. These settings can't be changed after the availability set is created.

notes.front: During planned maintenance, how many update domains are restarted at a time?
notes.back: Only one.
notes.explanation: The order might not be sequential, and a restarted update domain gets 30 minutes to recover before the next one starts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “Update domains” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The order of update domains being restarted might not proceed sequentially during planned maintenance, but only one update domain is restarted at a time. A restarted update domain has 30 minutes to recover before maintenance starts on a different update domain.

notes.front: An availability set has five update domains and six virtual machines. Which update domain does the sixth machine land in?
notes.back: The same update domain as the first machine.
notes.choices:
A) A new, sixth update domain
B) The same one as the first machine
C) The same one as the fifth machine
D) None: the set rejects it
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the set keeps the five domains it was created with. C and D don’t follow the documented wrap-round placement.
notes.explanation: Placement wraps round: the sixth joins the first, the seventh the second, and so on.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “Update domains” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If more than five VMs are configured in an availability set with five update domains, the sixth VM is placed in the same update domain as the first, the seventh with the second, and so on.

notes.front: How many virtual machines should an availability set contain to meet the 99.95% Azure service-level agreement?
notes.back: Two or more.
notes.explanation: Using two or more machines in the set helps keep the application highly available.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “What is an availability set?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you use availability sets, create two or more VMs within an availability set. Using two or more VMs in an availability set helps keep applications highly available and meets the 99.95% Azure service-level agreement (SLA).

notes.front: Does placing virtual machines in an availability set protect against operating system or application failures?
notes.back: No. It limits the impact of hardware failures, network outages and power interruptions.
notes.explanation: It protects against physical failures, not software ones.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “Fault domains” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Placing your virtual machines into an availability set doesn't protect your application from operating system or application-specific failures. But it does limit the impact of potential physical hardware failures, network outages, or power interruptions.

notes.front: You want two web servers in an availability set to survive the failure of one shared power supply and network switch. Which kind of domain separates them against that?
notes.back: Fault domains.
notes.choices:
A) Fault domains
B) Update domains
C) Resource groups
D) Subscriptions
notes.choicesExplained: B covers planned restarts, not power or switch failures. C and D are management containers, not physical separation.
notes.explanation: A fault domain is the group of machines sharing a common power source and network switch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “Fault domains” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Fault domains define the group of virtual machines that share a common power source and network switch.

notes.front: You don’t want planned platform maintenance to restart all your availability set’s web servers at once. Which kind of domain handles this?
notes.back: Update domains.
notes.choices:
A) Fault domains
B) Update domains
C) Availability zones only
D) Scale set autoscale
notes.choicesExplained: A separates machines by power and network hardware. C is a different option from an availability set. D changes machine counts, not maintenance order.
notes.explanation: Update domains group machines that can be restarted together, and maintenance restarts one update domain at a time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “Update domains” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Update domains indicate groups of virtual machines and underlying physical hardware that can be restarted at the same time.

notes.front: Availability sets or availability zones: which gives lower machine-to-machine latency, and which gives more resilience?
notes.back: Availability sets give lower latency; availability zones give higher resilience.
notes.explanation: Machines in a set sit physically closer, but sets don’t offer the resilience of zones.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability sets overview”, “What is an availability set?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Availability sets provide lower VM‑to‑VM latency than availability zones because the VMs are placed in closer physical proximity.

notes.front: Can a failure in one availability zone bring down a regional (non-zonal) virtual machine?
notes.back: Yes. A failure in any zone of the region can bring down a regional machine.
notes.explanation: There is no insight into which zone a regional resource is in.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability options for Azure Virtual Machines”, “Availability zones” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Regional resources may or may not exist in an Availability zone, and there is no insight into what physical or logical zone a regional resource is in. A failure in any of the availability zones in a region has the potential to bring down a regional VM.

notes.front: An application on virtual machines must keep running if a whole datacentre in the region is lost. What should you do?
notes.back: Deploy replicated machines across availability zones.
notes.choices:
A) Put them in one availability set
B) Deploy them across availability zones
C) Leave them regional
D) Use a larger size
notes.choicesExplained: A doesn’t give the resilience of zones. C can be brought down by a zone failure. D doesn’t add redundancy.
notes.explanation: Replicated machines in zones protect apps and data from the loss of a datacentre.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability options for Azure Virtual Machines”, “Availability zones” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By designing your solutions to use replicated VMs in zones, you can protect your apps and data from the loss of a data center.

notes.front: Scale sets or availability sets: which can automatically change the number of virtual machines in response to demand?
notes.back: Scale sets.
notes.explanation: Scale set instance counts can rise and fall with demand or a schedule, and are managed centrally.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability options for Azure Virtual Machines”, “Virtual Machines Scale Sets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The number of VM instances can automatically increase or decrease in response to demand or a defined schedule.

notes.front: Can you change a scale set’s orchestration mode after you create it?
notes.back: No. It is set at creation and can’t be changed or updated later.
notes.explanation: Choose Flexible or Uniform when you create the scale set.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The orchestration mode is defined when you create the scale set and cannot be changed or updated later.

notes.front: Which orchestration mode is recommended when deploying scale sets in Azure?
notes.back: Flexible orchestration.
notes.explanation: It is optimised for high availability and scalability with identical or mixed virtual machine types.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure”, “Scale Sets with Flexible Orchestration (Recommended)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Flexible Orchestration is the recommended orchestration mode when deploying scale sets in Azure.

notes.front: Which orchestration mode deploys identical instances from a predefined virtual machine profile and manages them mainly as a group?
notes.back: Uniform orchestration.
notes.explanation: It is optimised for large-scale workloads with identical instances.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure”, “Scale Sets with Uniform Orchestration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Uniform orchestration ensures consistency by using a predefined virtual machine profile to deploy identical instances within a scale set. While some customization of individual VMs is possible, Uniform orchestration primarily manages VMs as a group.

notes.front: Flexible or Uniform: in which scale set mode can Linux and Windows instances sit in the same scale set?
notes.back: Flexible. Uniform instances all use the same operating system.
notes.explanation: Flexible also allows mixing virtual machine types.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure”, “Basic setup” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Yes, Linux and Windows can reside in the same Flexible scale set  | No, instances are the same operating system

notes.front: Are Uniform scale set instances compatible with Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery?
notes.back: No. They lack compatibility with the standard virtual machine commands, tagging and those services.
notes.explanation: Uniform instances are reached through scale-set-specific commands instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure”, “Scale Sets with Uniform Orchestration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Individual instances are accessible via Virtual Machine Scale Set VM API commands but lack compatibility with standard Azure IaaS VM API commands, Azure Resource Manager tagging, RBAC, Azure Backup, or Azure Site Recovery.

notes.front: A new scale set must mix Spot and on-demand instances of different virtual machine types. Which orchestration mode do you choose at creation?
notes.back: Flexible orchestration.
notes.choices:
A) Uniform, then switch later
B) Flexible
C) Uniform
D) An availability set instead
notes.choicesExplained: A is impossible: the mode can’t change after creation. C deploys identical instances from one profile. D supports regular priority instances only.
notes.explanation: Flexible allows dynamic instance mixing, including Spot with on-demand, and the mode can’t be changed later.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure”, “Scale Sets with Flexible Orchestration (Recommended)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: it allows for dynamic instance mixing, enabling the use of different VM types, as well as a combination of Spot and on-demand instances, for optimized performance and cost efficiency.

notes.front: What does a zone-spanning scale set do?
notes.back: Spreads its instances across two or more availability zones.
notes.explanation: Spreading across zones is recommended for most workloads in Azure.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability zone options for Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Zone spanning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A zone-spanning scale set spreads instances across two or more availability zones.

notes.front: What is a zonal (single-zone) scale set mainly used for?
notes.back: Lower latency between instances, all placed in one availability zone.
notes.explanation: Each machine and its disks are pinned to that zone.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability zone options for Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Zonal or zone aligned (single zone)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A zonal or zone aligned scale set places instances in a single availability zone. Each VM and its disks are zonal, so they are pinned to a specific zone. This configuration is primarily used when you need lower latency between instances.

notes.front: In a regional (non-zonal) scale set, are instances pinned to availability zones or balanced across them?
notes.back: Neither. Instances aren’t pinned, and there is no guarantee of balance or spread across zones.
notes.explanation: You get a regional scale set by leaving zones unset.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability zone options for Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Regional (nonzonal)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In this configuration, the scale set creates regional (nonzonal, not zone-pinned) instances and implicitly places instances throughout the region. There is no guarantee for balance or spread across zones

notes.front: A scale set’s web tier must keep serving if one availability zone fails. Which zone deployment option fits?
notes.back: Zone spanning.
notes.choices:
A) Zonal (single zone)
B) Zone spanning
C) Regional (nonzonal)
D) One availability set
notes.choicesExplained: A puts every instance in the one zone that might fail. C gives no guarantee of spread, and a zone outage may affect any instance. D is not a scale set zone option.
notes.explanation: Spreading instances across zones is recommended for most workloads; if a zone fails, instances in the other zones should be unaffected.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Availability zone options for Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Zone spanning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the event of a zone outage or connectivity issue, connectivity to instances within the affected zone may be compromised, while instances in other availability zones should be unaffected.

notes.front: What are two host-based metrics you can use in scale set autoscale rules?
notes.back: Among others: Network In and Disk Read Bytes.
notes.explanation: Others include `Percentage CPU`, Network Out and Disk Write Bytes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Autoscale rule criteria” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The following host-based metrics are available for use when you create autoscale rules.

notes.front: Do host-based metrics for autoscale need an agent installed in the virtual machines?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: They give visibility into the machines’ performance without installing or configuring more agents.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Use host-based metrics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Host metrics give you visibility into the performance of the virtual machines in a scale set without the need to install or configure more agents and data collections.

notes.front: Which autoscale action suits a large scale set where adding a fixed number of machines may not noticeably help?
notes.back: Increase percent by.
notes.explanation: A fixed count, Increase count by, suits scale sets with fewer machines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Actions when rules trigger” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A percentage-based increase of virtual machines. Good for larger scale sets where a fixed increase may not noticeably improve performance.

notes.front: Why configure autoscale rules to scale in when demand stays low, such as in the evening?
notes.back: Scaling in cuts the cost of the scale set, because you run only the instances current demand needs.
notes.explanation: Scale-in rules are for decreases in load that are consistent over a period of time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Benefits of autoscale” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This scale-in action reduces the cost to run your scale set as you only run the number of instances required to meet the current demand.

notes.front: For demand you can predict, why can scheduled autoscale beat performance-based rules?
notes.back: Performance-based rules may let performance suffer before new machines are provisioned; scheduled rules have them ready in advance.
notes.explanation: Scheduled rules act at fixed times instead of waiting for a metric threshold.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Scheduled autoscale” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With performance-based rules, there may be a performance impact on the application before the autoscale rules trigger and the new virtual machines are provisioned. If you can anticipate such demand, the extra virtual machines are provisioned and ready for the increased customer use and application demand.

notes.front: An internal app is busy only in working hours on weekdays, and you want extra machines ready before staff arrive. Which kind of autoscale rule fits?
notes.back: A scheduled (schedule-based) autoscale rule.
notes.choices:
A) A metric rule on host-based metrics
B) A scheduled rule
C) Manual scaling each morning
D) A larger virtual machine size
notes.choicesExplained: A reacts only after load rises, so machines may not be ready. C works but isn’t automatic. D doesn’t change the number of machines.
notes.explanation: Schedule-based rules can scale out at the start of the working day and scale in at the end.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Scheduled autoscale” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Automatically scale out the number of virtual machines at the start of the work day when customer demand increases. At the end of the work day, automatically scale in the number of virtual machines to minimize resource costs overnight when application use is low.

notes.front: A public web shop gets unpredictable traffic surges that last for hours. You want the scale set to add machines when load stays high. What do you configure?
notes.back: Autoscale rules on metrics such as `Percentage CPU`, with a threshold and duration.
notes.choices:
A) Scheduled autoscale at fixed times
B) Metric-based autoscale rules
C) An availability set
D) Resize every machine to a larger size
notes.choicesExplained: A can’t predict when surges come. C doesn’t add machines. D doesn’t change the count and restarts running machines.
notes.explanation: Metric rules suit consistent increases in load, and you control the metric, how long it must hold, and how many machines to add.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Benefits of autoscale” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You control what metrics to monitor, such as CPU or memory, how long the application load must meet a given threshold, and how many virtual machines to add to the scale set.

notes.front: How do you manually change the number of instances in a scale set in the portal?
notes.back: Under Settings, Scaling: choose Manual Scale, update Instance count and select Save.
notes.explanation: Behind the scenes this updates the scale set’s sku.capacity property.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets”, “Manual scaling” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-compute-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can manually increase or decrease the number of instances in the virtual machine scale set by updating the `sku.capacity` property.
